summary: The respondent, serving as Head of Compliance for a mobility technology group regarding the Port Calder traffic signal system, demonstrates clear reflexivity and critical awareness regarding legal versus ethical risks. However, the account highlights acute negative polarities across the remaining Responsible Innovation dimensions. In terms of anticipation and responsiveness, the respondent identifies an inevitable infrastructural lock-in where fallback plans decay, leaving no viable capacity to halt or switch off the system. Furthermore, public engagement is entirely absent, characterized by a lack of community input or external oversight bodies, leaving compliance resting solely on internal document logging ('the risk register is where things go to be filed'). Multi-coding in the second segment captures how deterministic technical lock-in directly forecloses adaptive responsiveness.
transcript:
Interview transcript P04 — Head of compliance, mobility technology group
Case: Port Calder adaptive traffic signal and pedestrian detection system  |  SYNTHETIC DATA — not a real interview
[Interviewer] What does responsible deployment mean in your role?
[Respondent] In practice it means I am the person who asks the questions nobody wants asked, three weeks before launch, when it is expensive. I've made peace with being unpopular. The honest version is that most of what I do is legal risk, not ethics. Those overlap but they are not the same thing and I try not to pretend otherwise.
[Interviewer] What did you ask on this project?
[Respondent] Three things, mainly. What happens to footage of people who aren't the subject of any incident. Whether the detection performance is uniform across body types and mobility aids. And whether the city can switch it off if it turns out to be wrong. The third one is the one nobody has a good answer to, ever.
[Interviewer] What answer did you get on switching it off?
[Respondent] A version of 'why would we'. Which isn't an answer. Once the signal timing is adaptive, the fixed-time plans that used to run the junctions get out of date within a year or two — nobody maintains them any more. So the fallback decays. In two years turning it off means the traffic gets worse than it was before you started, and at that point nobody will turn it off. That is lock-in and it is happening quietly.
[Interviewer] Did that get escalated?
[Respondent] I wrote it up. It went into the risk register. The risk register is where things go to be filed. I don't think it reached anyone who could have changed the design, and I didn't push it beyond the register, which I'll own.
[Interviewer] Was there any external input into these questions?
[Respondent] No. It's me and a junior analyst. We don't have an ethics board, we don't have community input, we have me reading and worrying. For a system that watches thirty intersections that is a thin basis and I would say that on the record.
